column2: Don’t give honey under 1 year, or cough and cold medicines under 2 years unless a doctor advises.

Step-by-step preparation, storage and bottle feeding

Typical poo of a breastfed baby.
Mother and baby are treated together; don’t stop treatment early.
Most mothers make enough milk. The best signs are the baby’s nappies and weight gain.
Don’t keep leftover formula for the next feed.
Fever lasting more than 2 days
Give fever medicine only at the dose on the leaflet or recommended by your doctor for your baby’s weight.

Record the temperature and medicine time in Fever tracking.

Contact your doctor the same day

Feed little and often.

Keep an opened formula tin closed and dry; use it within the time on the pack.

Extreme sleepiness, floppiness

Painful swelling and redness in one leg
Do the glass test: press a clear glass on the rash; if it doesn’t fade, see a doctor at once.
Fainting or a fit
Vomiting after a knock to the head
Baby hasn’t regained birth weight by 2 weeks
Baby can’t feed at all because of pain
A baby may refuse the breast because of a blocked nose, earache, teething or distraction.
Baby falls asleep quickly at the breast and isn’t gaining weight
If the baby coughs, pulls off the breast or is very windy while feeding, the flow may be fast.
Baby isn’t gaining weight or is very unsettled
Baby can’t latch on
Baby is feeding much less than usual
Baby can’t keep fluids down or has vomited for more than 24 hours
Baby is sleepy and reluctant to feed
Babies may catch several colds a year; most clear up in 7–10 days.
Most baby rashes are harmless (baby acne, heat rash, nappy rash).
You think the baby may have tongue-tie
Hold the baby upright while feeding; throw away formula not finished within 2 hours.
Don’t put the baby in direct sun; sunlight doesn’t replace treatment.
Bring the baby to the breast with the mouth wide open; lower lip turned out, chin touching the breast.
White patches in the baby’s mouth that don’t wipe off and burning, stabbing nipple pain in the mother may be thrush.
Respect the baby’s fullness cues: turning the head, slowing sucking, pushing the bottle away.
Change position so the baby’s chin points towards the lump.
Feel your baby’s movements every day. If the usual pattern changes, don’t wait until tomorrow; you can also track them with the kick counter.
If symptoms don’t improve in 12–24 hours, see a doctor the same day; antibiotics may be needed.
If you have these signs, see a doctor for both mother and baby.
Keep the baby upright for 20–30 minutes after feeds.
Bringing up a little milk after feeds (posseting) is normal. Vomiting is larger and more forceful.
While feeding
Make eye contact and hold the baby in your arms while feeding.
White, grey or clay-coloured
Wash your hands well after changing nappies.
